2.1.learning_target: Students will explain that motion is relative and describe an object’s motion using an appropriate frame of reference.
i_cans: I can explain why an object can be moving relative to one reference frame but not another.
I can identify the reference frame used in a motion description.
I can compare motion from two different points of view and explain why everyday motion is usually described relative to Earth’s surface.
2.1.misconceptions_text: Treating motion as absolute | Switching reference frames mid-explanation | Omitting what the motion is measured relative to

2.2.learning_target: Students will distinguish between speed and velocity and use distance, time, and direction to describe motion.
i_cans: I can calculate average speed from distance and time.
I can distinguish instantaneous speed from average speed.
I can explain that velocity includes both speed and direction and compare examples of constant speed, constant velocity, and changing velocity.
2.2.misconceptions_text: Using speed and velocity as synonyms | Reporting velocity without direction | Confusing instantaneous and average speed
2.2.recurring_practices: quantitative reasoning; data interpretation; communication with units

2.3.learning_target: Students will explain acceleration as the rate at which velocity changes and identify acceleration from motion descriptions, data, and graphs.
i_cans: I can calculate acceleration from change in velocity and time.
I can explain that acceleration can involve speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction.
I can identify positive, negative, or zero acceleration from a motion situation and interpret simple motion graphs and connect them to velocity or acceleration.
2.3.misconceptions_text: Defining acceleration only as speeding up | Using sign alone to decide speeding up or slowing down | Confusing velocity with acceleration
2.3.recurring_practices: graph/data interpretation; quantitative reasoning; model translation

2.4.learning_target: Students will describe free fall as motion under the influence of gravity alone and use simple free-fall relationships to determine speed or distance fallen.
i_cans: I can explain why objects in free fall accelerate at the same rate when air resistance is ignored.
I can use $g \approx 10\text{ m/s}^2$ to determine speed gained during free fall.
I can use free-fall patterns to compare distance fallen during different time intervals and distinguish free fall from falling with significant air resistance.
2.4.misconceptions_text: Believing heavier objects fall faster in ideal free fall | Treating any falling object as free fall | Confusing $g$ with speed
2.4.recurring_practices: mathematical reasoning; model evaluation; explanation of phenomena

2.5.learning_target: Students will use velocity vectors, motion diagrams, and simple graphs to model and explain the motion of objects.
i_cans: I can represent velocity with arrows that show both speed and direction.
I can compare velocity vectors to determine whether an object’s velocity is changing.
I can connect motion diagrams, data tables, and graphs to written descriptions of motion and critique an incorrect motion model and revise it using evidence.
2.5.misconceptions_text: Treating vector direction as optional | Matching graph height to physical height | Failing to distinguish position velocity and acceleration representations
2.5.recurring_practices: develop/evaluate models; representation translation; argument from evidence
